summary: BBN's announcement of a new proposed File Transfer Protocol document and a meeting at BBN on March 16 to try for final agreement. The proposal is an extensive update to RFC 354 intended to address objections raised against it. It is a proposal and meeting call, not a final standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone rewrote the rules for sending files between computers and invited everyone interested to a meeting to agree on them. This note is the invitation and the new draft.

subtitle: A meeting call and a rewritten FTP proposal meant to settle the objections raised against RFC 354.

tldr.problem: RFC 354 had drawn objections, and its author wanted another attempt at final agreement on a File Transfer Protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The memo attaches a proposed document that extensively updates RFC 354, and calls a meeting at BBN on March 16 to discuss it and other proposals.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposal and meeting announcement, not a final standard. The unit metadata lists it as updating RFC 354.

sections.title: The Meeting Announcement
sections.content:
Alex McKenzie of BBN says the attached document is an extensive update to RFC 354 and, he believes, solves most of the objections to it. He calls a meeting of interested parties at BBN on March 16 to discuss this and other proposals.

The note is aimed at the whole network community, not only the old FTP committee, because the committee did not include everyone who had contributed to FTP. Attendees should already know RFC 354 and also RFC 385, RFC 414, RFC 418 and RFC 438. The proposed document itself came out of a meeting on 25 January 1973 with seven named participants from MIT and BBN.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says: here is a better draft, please come to a meeting so we can finally agree on it.

sections.title: The FTP Model
sections.content:
File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is a protocol for transferring files between hosts on the ARPA Network, including terminal IMPs. Its goals are to promote sharing of files, encourage indirect use of remote computers, shield a user from the differences between host file systems, and transfer data reliably and efficiently. It is usable at a terminal but designed mainly for use by programs.

The model uses two kinds of connection. A user-TELNET opens TELNET connections to the server on socket 3, and commands and replies travel over them in ASCII. A separate, simplex data connection carries the file itself; it may run in either direction, need not exist all the time, and may be in use twice at once, once each way. The user listens on a data socket, and the server initiates the data connection in the byte size, mode and type that were negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: One connection carries the conversation and the instructions; a second, separate connection carries the file. The person receiving the file opens the door first, and the other computer knocks and sends it.

sections.title: Commands, Types and What Changed
sections.content:
Commands are ASCII strings ending in CRLF, starting with a code of four or fewer letters. They set access control (USER, PASS, ACCT, REIN, BYE), transfer parameters (BYTE, SOCK, LSTN, TYPE, FORM, STRU, MODE) or a service request (RETR, STOR, APPE, ALLO, REST, RNFR, RNTO, ABOR, DELE, LIST, NLST, STAT, HELP, MLFL, MAIL). The representation types are ASCII, EBCDIC, Image and Local Byte, and the transfer modes are Stream, Text, Block and Hasp. Servers send three-digit reply codes whose first digit says whether the reply is informative, a success, an incomplete answer, a failure, or an illegal command.

Compared with RFC 354, servers are now required, not merely advised, to implement the 8-bit byte size; EBCDIC is its own representation type; in ASCII representation any byte size other than 8 bits cancels the transfer request; and the RFC states that an EOF does not imply an EOR. A declarative section fixes the minimum server implementation and the initial defaults (ASCII type, Stream mode, File structure, Unformatted).
sections.plainLanguage: The commands set who you are, how the file is shaped and encoded, and what to do with it. Several soft suggestions in the old draft became firm requirements, and the smallest acceptable server is spelled out.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content:
The RFC ends with worked scenarios. In the first, a TIP user opens TELNET connections by ICP to host X on socket 3, logs in with USER and PASS, names a data socket with SOCK 65538, and requests a file with RETR this.file. Host X replies with its own data socket in a 255 SOCK 5533 reply, starts the transfer, and the user ends with BYE.

A second scenario shows a user-FTP program prompting a person through a session and failing a STOR with reply 451 Access denied. The conventions in the examples, such as '---->' for commands and '<----' for replies, are the RFC's own.
sections.plainLanguage: It walks through a whole session: log in, say where the file should go, ask for the file, and say goodbye.
